progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: B5b: homologous pairs, crossing over in prophase I makes new combinations of existing alleles, independent assortment at metaphase I, 2 to the power n (2 to the power 23 is more than 8 million), fertilisation restores the number, and letters are labels only. B5a: diploid, haploid, chromosome sets. B4: a copying error that survives proofreading and repair is a mutation, inherited only if it is in a cell that makes gametes. B7: genotype, phenotype, the same genotype in different environments, and the environment does not change the genotype. B2b: pollen tube, ovule, a pea pod's seeds are fertilised ovules. B1: clones, runners and variation helps a species survive change. Not assumed: tracing alleles across generations, genes on one chromosome travelling together, multiplying gamete types, genetic against environmental variation.
progression.startsWith: A pea pod whose seeds all have the same two parents yet differ, with the question of why offspring differ and whether one could carry an allele neither parent had.
progression.stopsAfter: Sorting the four sources into reshuffling existing alleles and making new alleles; tracing a parent's alleles to its own parents and listing four gamete types for two genes on different chromosomes with the assumptions stated; explaining why genes on the same chromosome are reshuffled only by crossing over and why those combinations are usually less common; multiplying gamete types at fertilisation; explaining why siblings share alleles but differ; saying mutation is the only source of new alleles and is inherited only from the egg or sperm line; separating genetic from environmental variation; saying why variation matters; applying all of it to an unseen fly cell and an unseen strawberry experiment. No linkage maps, no dominance or Punnett squares, no mutation types, no non-disjunction.
progression.nextLesson: P02: model meiosis, fertilisation and mutation yourself; then B9: predict offspring with Punnett squares and pedigrees.

teaching.task: Explain where the differences between offspring of the same parents come from, and where a brand-new allele comes from.
teaching.causalExplanation: Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation only rearrange alleles that already exist, like dealing new hands from the same deck, while mutation changes the DNA itself, so it is the only source of a new allele. A parent that got one set of chromosomes from each of its own parents makes four kinds of gamete for two genes on different chromosomes because each pair lines up either way on its own. Assortment moves whole chromosomes, so two genes on the same chromosome stay together until a swap between them, which happens in only some cells, so the swapped combinations are usually less common. Any pollen grain can reach any ovule, so fertilisation multiplies the gamete types. Siblings share alleles but differ because each came from different gametes, with no new mutation needed. A mutation is inherited only if it is in a cell that makes eggs or sperm. Environmental differences between clones are not inherited because the environment does not change the alleles in the gametes.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on a pod of different seeds from the same two parents, sorts the four sources by whether they reshuffle or make something new, traces one parent's alleles back and forward on one origin board, adds the same-chromosome case, multiplies at fertilisation, explains siblings and mutation with the white-eyed fly, separates genetic from environmental variation, says why variation matters, gives the memory aid, then asks two harder unseen items with a short pause and brief model answers.
teaching.openingDecision: Seeds from one pod have the same two parents, yet they differ. Why, and where could a brand-new allele come from?
teaching.understandingCheck: A cell in a fruit fly's ovary has D and E on one chromosome, d and e on its partner, and F and f on another pair: list the egg combinations with no crossing over, the extra ones with crossing over between D and E, and why those are less common. Then explain the variation in strawberry plants grown from runners against plants grown from seeds, and say which differences could be passed on through seeds.
teaching.curriculumScope: Model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis and the knowledge half of the investigation of crossing over, fertilisation and mutation (Module 5, B5-IQ4-01 and B5-IQ4-02, ACSBL084). The video models on screen and does not claim learner modelling. Linkage maps, dominance, Punnett squares, mutation types and non-disjunction are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, painted ovary, pod, pea seed, fly, hydrangea, strawberry, sperm and egg plates, the B5b dividing cell plate with plum and teal chromosome plates, and coded allele beads, an origin board of three generation rows, a pairing grid, number tickers and a variation split. Allele beads are white with an outline and a letter; amber is reserved for a new allele and only a mutation bead is ever amber-filled.
design.transitionPlan: The pod opens the lesson and crossfades from the ovary; the source chips sort into two bins; the origin board draws in three rows and persists from the tracing scene to the siblings scene, zooming to the long pair for the same-chromosome scene; the ovary and pod return for fertilisation; the DNA ladder and the fly jar carry mutation; the variation split carries the genetic against environmental scene; each attempt card clears the aids and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the next chips slide in; scene crossfade with settle.
